rv.q: Allison Crutchfield’s recreations of their iconic suits, stylish but a little too tight, perfectly convey a duo in limbo: no longer schoolboys, not yet legends.
This show is so appealing, it is sure to sell out. Get your tickets while you can.
Stevens arrives at the true impetus for his not only charming but indisputably touching work.
Only Yesterday is an enthralling experience that allows us to revel in our own memories of how much we, too, love the Beatles.
Stevens' play rises and falls on its own merits, which are just enough to make this slight entertainment enjoyable for even the most casual Beatles fan. But the play could have been a lot more.

It's thanks largely to the energy, facility and immense charm of these actors—and director Carol Dunne's light, sure hand and obvious affection for the subject matter—that Stevens's slight, often predictable account works as well as it does here.
Only Yesterday is lovely and sweet in its desire to give more and let us see more.
There's really not much of a play in this 70-minute exercise, uninspiringly directed by Carol Dunne...

'Only Yesterday' is Bob Stevens's first play. Prior work has focused on producing, writing, and consulting for television sitcoms. His lack of experience is evident here. It is difficult for Mr. Crawford and Mr. Sears to tackle this anemic script with any chance of overcoming its myriad deficiencies.

cn.t: Critics find this imagined Beatles encounter charming but uneven, with sensitive performances and elegant storytelling praised, though some dismiss it as disappointingly slight and lacking fresh insights into the iconic duo.
